clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic ACSF3 variants encoding a mitochondrial acyl-CoA synthetase that activates malonate and methylmalonate.

Defined biochemically by simultaneous elevation of both malonic and methylmalonic acids, with methylmalonate usually higher than malonate, the reverse of the ratio seen in malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency.
The phenotype is highly variable: some individuals present in childhood with developmental delay, seizures or faltering growth, while others remain asymptomatic or first present in adulthood.
Adult presentations may include cognitive decline, memory disturbance, psychiatric symptoms, encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy or seizures.
Plasma malonylcarnitine is typically normal or only marginally raised, so the condition is easily missed on acylcarnitine-based newborn screening.
Methylmalonate is elevated with normal methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity and normal cobalamin metabolism, distinguishing it from classic methylmalonic acidaemia.
ACSF3 participates in mitochondrial fatty-acid synthesis, including the endogenous production of lipoic acid precursors, which may contribute to the phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: ACSF3 encodes a mitochondrial acyl-CoA synthetase (acyl-CoA synthetase family member 3) that activates malonic and methylmalonic acid to their CoA esters within the mitochondrion, a step in mitochondrial fatty-acid synthesis that also feeds the endogenous production of lipoic acid. Loss of ACSF3 function impairs the mitochondrial handling and utilisation of malonate and methylmalonate, so both accumulate and are excreted in the urine; because the block is downstream of and distinct from methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and cobalamin metabolism, the methylmalonate elevation occurs with normal mutase activity and normal vitamin B12 handling. The relatively mild and variable phenotype is thought to reflect the partial and tissue-dependent consequences of impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid and lipoic-acid synthesis rather than a severe acute toxic organic acidaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency (MLYCD), the sibling malonate disorder, but with malonate exceeding methylmalonate and prominent cardiomyopathy
Classic methylmalonic acidaemia (MMUT / methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency)
Cobalamin (vitamin B12) metabolism defects and dietary B12 deficiency causing methylmalonate elevation
SUCLA2 and SUCLG1 disorders and other mitochondrial diseases with mild methylmalonate elevation
Other causes of adult-onset leukoencephalopathy or cognitive and psychiatric decline
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids (both malonate and methylmalonate raised, with attention to the ratio)
Plasma and urine methylmalonic acid quantification
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (malonylcarnitine often normal, hence easily missed)
Serum vitamin B12, plasma homocysteine and cobalamin/mutase studies to exclude classic methylmalonic acidaemia
Brain MRI in symptomatic cases, especially adults with neurological features
redFlags: Unexplained progressive cognitive decline, encephalopathy or new psychiatric symptoms in an adult with combined malonate and methylmalonate elevation
Seizures or neurological regression in a child
Emerging peripheral neuropathy or focal neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Many individuals have a mild course or remain asymptomatic, but a subset, including some adults, develop significant neurological or neuropsychiatric disease; the full natural history is still being defined and prognosis is correspondingly uncertain.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because malonylcarnitine is normal and newborn screening does not flag it.
Misclassifying the methylmalonate elevation as classic methylmalonic acidaemia or as vitamin B12 deficiency.
Overlooking the condition in adults presenting with unexplained cognitive or psychiatric decline.
Failing to note that methylmalonate exceeds malonate, which distinguishes it from malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency.
references: Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
Organic acidurias and mitochondrial fatty-acid synthesis reviews
management: Management is largely supportive, as no proven disease-specific therapy exists
Symptomatic treatment of seizures with antiepileptic drugs, alongside developmental and educational support for affected children
Assessment and management of neuropsychiatric and neurological features, including cognitive decline and peripheral neuropathy, in adults
Involve a metabolic dietitian, recognising that trials of protein or substrate modification remain of unproven benefit
Monitoring with urine organic acids and clinical review, with brain MRI where neurological features emerge
Confirm the diagnosis by ACSF3 analysis and offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition
Long-term follow-up under a metabolic medicine specialist given the incompletely defined natural history
